# Profiling C and C++ code

> **Install for this page:** `pip install scope-profiler` supplies the C/C++
> sources. Building the examples requires a C99 compiler (and a C++11 compiler
> for the RAII wrapper); no Python extra is required.

scope-profiler ships a C region API with the same model as the Python one. A C
program marks regions and writes one file per rank at `sp_finalize()`, so a C
run gets the same summaries, charts, exporters and `plot` workflow as a Python
one.

Built with HDF5 — the preferred output format — that file *is* the profile:
`<prefix>_rank<NNNNN>.h5`, the same layout a Python run writes, opened
directly by `scope-profiler inspect`/`plot` and `read_h5()`. Without HDF5 the
program writes a compact `.spt` trace instead, which `scope-profiler
import-native` converts afterwards. See [Output format](#output-format).

The compiled backend is a small C99 entry source plus adjacent headers: with
no dependencies beyond libc, no MPI, and nothing else to link unless you opt
into HDF5. Keep the shipped `scope_profiler_impl.h` and
`scope_profiler_hdf5.h` beside `scope_profiler.c` when vendoring them. The
public header is `extern "C"`, so C++ codes can include it directly -- or
reach for the optional `scope_profiler.hpp` RAII wrapper described below.

C++ projects can instead use the C++17 header-only backend, and CMake projects
can consume exported `scope-profiler::native`, `scope-profiler::cpp`, and
`scope-profiler::header-only` targets.

The trace format is shared with {doc}`the Fortran API <fortran>`, so a program
built from both lands in a single profile — and so does a run whose ranks
wrote different formats.

## Getting the source

It ships inside the installed package:

```bash
cc -c $(python -c "import scope_profiler.native_trace as t; print(t.c_source_path())") \
   -I$(python -c "import scope_profiler.native_trace as t; print(t.c_include_dir())")
```

or from a checkout, `src/scope_profiler/c/`. A `Makefile` and a runnable
`example.c` sit next to it.

## Marking regions

```c
#include "scope_profiler.h"

int main(void)
{
    int step, solve, assemble;

    sp_init("profile", 0);              /* prefix, MPI rank */

    solve = sp_region("solve");         /* resolve names once... */
    assemble = sp_region("assemble");

    for (step = 0; step < nsteps; ++step) {
        sp_begin(assemble);             /* ...then use the handles */
        assemble_matrix();
        sp_end(assemble);

        sp_begin(solve);
        solve_system();
        sp_end(solve);
    }

    sp_finalize();                      /* writes profile_rank00000.h5 */
    return 0;
}
```

Regions may nest, and a region may re-enter itself recursively — each entry
reserves its own slot, exactly as in the Python API.

Nesting must be *proper*: a region entered inside another has to be left
before it. Post-processing reconstructs the call graph from the recorded
intervals, so a `sp_begin`/`sp_end` pair that crosses another region's
boundary — rather than sitting inside or outside it — has no call stack to
recover, and reading the trace back raises `NestingError`. The timings
themselves are still recorded and readable; it is the nesting, the flame
chart and the exclusive times that cannot be derived.

## The API

The default-context convenience functions:

| Call | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `int sp_init(const char *prefix, int rank)` | Start profiling. Returns non-zero if no monotonic clock is available. |
| `int sp_region(const char *name)` | Handle for a region name, created on first use. |
| `int sp_region_at(const char *name, const char *file, int line)` | Like `sp_region()`, also recording where it is defined. |
| `void sp_begin(int region)` / `void sp_end(int region)` | Enter and leave a region. |
| `int64_t sp_num_calls(int region)` | How often a region was entered; readable after `sp_finalize()`. |
| `int64_t sp_now_ns(void)` | The raw clock, in nanoseconds. Shared by every profiler. |
| `int sp_is_active(void)` | Whether profiling is running. |
| `int sp_finalize(void)` | Write `<prefix>_rank<NNNNN>.h5` (or `.spt`) and stop. Returns non-zero on write failure. |
| `int sp_set_output_format(sp_output_format)` | Choose HDF5 or trace output; see [Output format](#output-format). |
| `sp_output_format sp_current_output_format(void)` / `const char *sp_output_path(void)` | What will be written, and where. |

Calls made before `sp_init()` are harmless: `sp_region()` returns
`SP_INVALID_REGION` and `sp_begin`/`sp_end` ignore it. Instrumentation can stay
in a build that never profiles, with no `#ifdef` at the call sites.

The explicit-context API, each taking an `sp_profiler *` from `sp_create()`:

| Call | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `sp_profiler *sp_create(const char *prefix, int rank)` / `void sp_destroy(sp_profiler *)` | Create and release a profiler instance. |
| `int sp_profiler_region(sp_profiler *, const char *name)` | Handle for a region name, created on first use. |
| `int sp_profiler_region_at(sp_profiler *, const char *name, const char *file, int line)` | Like above, also recording where it is defined. |
| `void sp_profiler_begin(sp_profiler *, int region)` / `void sp_profiler_end(sp_profiler *, int region)` | Enter and leave a region. |
| `int sp_profiler_end_last(sp_profiler *)` | End whichever call, in any region, was opened most recently. |
| `sp_scope sp_profiler_scope_begin(sp_profiler *, int region)` / `int sp_scope_end(sp_scope *)` | A checked token for one exact call. |
| `int sp_profiler_reset(sp_profiler *)` | Discard recorded calls and statistics; keep region handles valid. |
| `int sp_profiler_get_region_stats(const sp_profiler *, int region, sp_region_stats *)` | Call count, total/min/max duration. |
| `int sp_profiler_num_regions(const sp_profiler *)` / `const char *sp_profiler_region_name(const sp_profiler *, int)` | Enumerate registered regions. |
| `int sp_profiler_flush(sp_profiler *)` | Write what has been recorded so far, without stopping profiling. |
| `int sp_profiler_finalize(sp_profiler *)` | Write the output file and stop. |
| `int sp_profiler_set_output_format(sp_profiler *, sp_output_format)` / `sp_output_format sp_profiler_output_format(const sp_profiler *)` | The format this profiler writes. |
| `int sp_profiler_is_active(const sp_profiler *)` / `const char *sp_profiler_output_path(const sp_profiler *)` | Introspection. |
| `sp_status sp_profiler_last_error(const sp_profiler *)` / `const char *sp_error_string(sp_status)` | What went wrong, if anything. |

Every one of these accepts a `NULL` or inactive profiler harmlessly, the same
way the default-context functions tolerate calls before `sp_init()`.

## Multiple profilers: explicit contexts

`sp_init()`/`sp_region()`/`sp_begin()`/`sp_end()`/`sp_finalize()` all operate
on one hidden default profiler per process. Library code that must not
interfere with a caller's own profiling -- or with another instance of
itself -- creates its own instead:

```c
sp_profiler *p = sp_create("solver", rank);

int solve = sp_profiler_region(p, "solve");
sp_profiler_begin(p, solve);
solve_system();
sp_profiler_end(p, solve);

sp_profiler_finalize(p);   /* writes solver_rank00000.h5 */
sp_destroy(p);
```

Every `sp_create()`d instance owns its own regions, buffers and open calls;
nothing about one can corrupt another. `sp_create()` never returns `NULL`
except on outright allocation failure -- if no clock is available, it hands
back a profiler that is simply inactive (every call against it a harmless
no-op, same as the default context before `sp_init()`), so check
`sp_profiler_is_active()` or `sp_profiler_last_error()` rather than a `NULL`
return.

## A checked call token

`sp_begin()`/`sp_end()` identify a call only by region, so an incorrectly
ordered `sp_end()` is caught only later, on import. `sp_profiler_scope_begin()`
returns a token for the exact call instead:

```c
sp_scope call = sp_profiler_scope_begin(p, solve);
solve_system();
sp_scope_end(&call);
```

Ending a token whose call is not the innermost one open in its region is
refused (`SP_ERR_UNMATCHED_END`) rather than mistiming whichever call
actually is -- the token stays valid, so ending it again later, once it is on
top, succeeds normally. Ending it twice is harmless: the second call finds
nothing left to end. This is what a C++ RAII wrapper should store per scope,
since a moved-from token is naturally inert.

For code that tracks "the currently open section" itself instead of naming a
region to close it, `sp_profiler_end_last(p)` ends whichever call -- in any region --
was opened most recently and not yet closed.

## Source-aware registration

`sp_region_at()` records where a region is defined alongside its name, using
the same `(source_file, source_line)` shape `scope-profiler`'s own source
navigation and exports already understand:

```c
int solve = sp_profiler_region_at(p, "solve", __FILE__, __LINE__);
```

It exists on both the default context (`sp_region_at`) and explicit ones
(`sp_profiler_region_at`). A name registered without a source location (via
`sp_region()`, or `sp_region_at()` called with `NULL`) can still pick one up
later -- the next `sp_region_at()` call for that name backfills it onto the
existing handle -- but once a handle has a location, later calls never
overwrite it.

`SP_REGION_AT(name)` / `SP_PROFILER_REGION_AT(profiler, name)` are macros
that fill in `__FILE__`/`__LINE__` for you:

```c
int solve = SP_REGION_AT("solve");                    /* default context */
int solve = SP_PROFILER_REGION_AT(p, "solve");         /* explicit context */
```

## C++: RAII scopes

`scope_profiler.hpp`, next to the C header, wraps a checked scope token in a
move-only C++11 class so a region is left however its scope exits --
`return`, `break`, or an exception -- instead of a hand-written
`sp_begin`/`sp_end` pair (or a hand-written wrapper of one's own):

```cpp
#include "scope_profiler.hpp"

sp_profiler *p = sp_create("solver", rank);
int solve = sp_profiler_region(p, "solve");

void step()
{
    sp::Scope timed(p, solve);
    solve_system();   // sp_scope_end() runs on every exit path, throw included
}
```

Against the default context instead of an explicit one, drop the profiler
argument:

```cpp
sp_init("profile", rank);
int solve = sp_region("solve");
...
sp::Scope timed(solve);
```

It is header-only and pulls in nothing beyond `scope_profiler.h`, so it never
needs to be compiled or linked on its own -- only included from C++
translation units. `make hpp-check` (in `src/scope_profiler/c/`) compile-checks
it in CI.

### Scoped instrumentation macros

The recommended C++ call-site API captures source locations and closes regions
on every exit path:

```cpp
void solve()
{
    SP_PROFILE_FUNCTION();
    SP_PROFILE_SCOPE("assemble");
    assemble_matrix();
}
```

`SP_PROFILE_SCOPE_CTX(profiler, "assemble")` and
`SP_PROFILE_FUNCTION_CTX(profiler)` select an explicit profiler. Give each
macro its own lexical scope when two invocations would otherwise be on the
same source line.

Define `SP_DISABLE_PROFILING` for an uninstrumented build. All four macros then
expand to no-ops: their arguments are not evaluated, their strings are not
retained, and no profiler symbol is referenced. The same source can therefore
remain instrumented without linking scope-profiler:

```bash
c++ -DSP_DISABLE_PROFILING application.cpp -o application
```

### C++17 header-only backend

Defining `SP_HEADER_ONLY` before including `scope_profiler.hpp` supplies inline
definitions of the complete recording backend. It is safe across multiple
translation units and needs no separately compiled `scope_profiler.c`:

```cpp
#define SP_HEADER_ONLY
#include "scope_profiler.hpp"
```

This mode requires C++17 for inline process-wide state. The ordinary compiled
backend and RAII wrapper continue to support C++11.

### Native LIKWID counters

Define `SP_USE_LIKWID` and `LIKWID_PERFMON`, include LIKWID's headers, and link
`liblikwid`. `SP_PROFILE_SCOPE*` then starts and stops a LIKWID marker with the
same name as its timing region. An RAII session owns LIKWID initialization and
finalization without involving Python:

```cpp
#define SP_USE_LIKWID
#include "scope_profiler.hpp"

int main()
{
    sp::LikwidSession counters;
    sp_init("profile", 0);
    {
        SP_PROFILE_SCOPE("solve");
        solve();
    }
    return sp_finalize();
}
```

Run the executable under `likwid-perfctr -m`. Worker threads must call
`sp::likwid_thread_init()` once before entering markers. The optional CMake
target described below supplies the definitions, include directory, and
library automatically.

## CMake package

An installed source distribution exports namespaced targets:

```cmake
find_package(scope-profiler CONFIG REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(simulation PRIVATE scope-profiler::cpp)
```

- `scope-profiler::native` is the compiled C99 recorder.
- `scope-profiler::cpp` adds the C++11 RAII/macro API and links the recorder.
- `scope-profiler::header-only` selects the C++17 header-only recorder.
- `scope-profiler::likwid` is available when scope-profiler was configured
  with `-DSCOPE_PROFILER_ENABLE_LIKWID=ON`; link this add-on alongside either
  `scope-profiler::cpp` or `scope-profiler::header-only`.
- `scope-profiler::mpi` similarly adds `scope_profiler_mpi.hpp` and MPI linkage
  when configured with `-DSCOPE_PROFILER_ENABLE_MPI=ON`.
- `-DSCOPE_PROFILER_ENABLE_HDF5=ON` needs no separate target: it puts
  `SP_USE_HDF5` and the HDF5 link on `scope-profiler::native` and
  `scope-profiler::header-only`, so everything built against them writes
  `.h5` profiles. See [Output format](#output-format).

The same targets work through `FetchContent_MakeAvailable(scope-profiler)`.
See `examples/cmake/` for both the installed-package and FetchContent paths.

## Reset, statistics and flushing

`sp_profiler_reset()` discards every recorded call and each region's
statistics but keeps every region name and handle valid, so a long-running
application can report periodically without re-resolving anything:

```c
sp_region_stats stats;
sp_profiler_get_region_stats(p, solve, &stats);
printf("solve: %lld calls, %lld ns total\n",
       (long long)stats.calls, (long long)stats.total_ns);

sp_profiler_reset(p);   /* refuses with SP_ERR_OPEN_SCOPES if solve is still open */
```

`sp_profiler_flush(p)` writes everything recorded so far to the trace file
without stopping profiling -- a call still open is simply left out until a
later flush or `sp_profiler_finalize()` includes it.

## Errors

Every explicit-context function accepts a `NULL` or inactive profiler
harmlessly, and records what went wrong on the profiler itself:

```c
if (sp_profiler_last_error(p) != SP_OK) {
    fprintf(stderr, "scope_profiler: %s\n",
            sp_error_string(sp_profiler_last_error(p)));
}
```

`sp_profiler_output_path(p)` returns the path `sp_profiler_finalize()` /
`sp_profiler_flush()` write (or wrote), so callers do not need to reconstruct
`<prefix>_rank<NNNNN>.h5` — or `.spt` — themselves.

## Output format

`sp_finalize()` writes one file per rank, in one of two formats.

**HDF5 — preferred.** `<prefix>_rank<NNNNN>.h5` is an ordinary
scope-profiler profile, byte-layout-identical to what a Python run writes, so
there is nothing to convert:

```bash
./simulation
scope-profiler inspect profile_rank00000.h5
scope-profiler plot default profile_rank00000.h5 -o figures
```

It is opt-in at compile time, because it is the only thing that gives the
library a dependency. Define `SP_USE_HDF5` and link `libhdf5`:

```bash
cc -std=c99 -O2 -DSP_USE_HDF5 -c scope_profiler.c $(pkg-config --cflags hdf5)
cc -O2 main.o scope_profiler.o $(pkg-config --libs hdf5) -o simulation
```

or, under CMake, `-DSCOPE_PROFILER_ENABLE_HDF5=ON`, which puts the definition
and the link on the `scope-profiler::native` and `scope-profiler::header-only`
targets for you. Serial HDF5 is enough — each rank writes its own file, so
nothing here needs parallel HDF5 or MPI.

**Trace — the fallback.** Without `SP_USE_HDF5` the program writes
`<prefix>_rank<NNNNN>.spt`, the compact binary trace shared with
{doc}`the Fortran API <fortran>`, and `scope-profiler import-native` turns it
into the same HDF5 output afterwards. It needs nothing but libc, which is what
makes it the right choice where the profiled machine has no HDF5 to link, or
where the run must not carry the library at all.

A build with HDF5 defaults to it, so most programs never touch the format API.
To pin one explicitly:

```c
sp_init("profile", rank);
sp_set_output_format(SP_OUTPUT_TRACE);   /* or SP_OUTPUT_HDF5 */
printf("writing %s\n", sp_output_path());
```

`sp_hdf5_available()` reports whether this build has the HDF5 backend at all.
Asking a build without it for `SP_OUTPUT_HDF5` returns `SP_ERR_UNSUPPORTED`
and leaves the format alone, so instrumentation that always asks for HDF5
still runs — and still produces a trace — where it is not available.

Both formats record exactly the same measurements. The difference is what the
file already is: an HDF5 profile carries the region names, source locations,
per-event timestamps and the fixed-size summary statistics a reader needs,
while a trace carries the names, source locations and timestamps and lets the
import derive the rest.

## Under MPI

Pass each rank's id so the output files do not collide:

```c
int rank;
MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, &rank);
sp_init("profile", rank);
```

Every rank writes its own file; nothing is communicated, so `sp_finalize()` is
not collective and a rank that dies takes only its own output with it. Merging
the ranks into one profile is a post-processing step, in either format:

```bash
mpirun -n 128 ./simulation
scope-profiler import-native . -o profiling_data.h5
scope-profiler plot default profiling_data.h5 -o figures
```

`import-native` reads both, and mixes them: it picks up `*.spt` traces and
per-rank `*_rank<NNNNN>.h5` profiles from a directory and merges every rank it
finds into one file. A merged profile sitting in the same directory is left
alone — only the per-rank naming is treated as input — so re-running the
import does not fold a previous result back into the next one.

With one rank there is nothing to merge: an HDF5 build's output file is the
profile, and `import-native` is only worth running to rename it.

## Python calling C

The case this is really for. Compile the kernels and the profiler into one
shared library and load it with `ctypes` — no binding generator, no build
backend:

```bash
cc -std=c99 -O2 -fPIC -shared kernels.c $(python -c \
    "import scope_profiler.native_trace as t; print(t.c_source_path())") \
   -I$(python -c "import scope_profiler.native_trace as t; print(t.c_include_dir())") \
   -o libkernels.so
```

```python
import ctypes
from scope_profiler import ProfileManager

kernels = ctypes.CDLL("./libkernels.so")
kernels.kernels_jacobi_solve.argtypes = [ctypes.c_int, ctypes.c_int]
kernels.kernels_jacobi_solve.restype = ctypes.c_double   # see the trap below

ProfileManager.setup(file_path="profiling_data.h5")
kernels.kernels_start_profiling(b"trace", 0)

for step in range(nsteps):
    with ProfileManager.region("python:step"):
        kernels.kernels_jacobi_solve(n, sweeps)          # records its own regions

kernels.kernels_stop_profiling()                          # writes the C output
ProfileManager.finalize(native_traces=".")                # ...and folds it in
```

**One file comes out**, `profiling_data.h5`, holding both languages — there is
no merge step here, and none of this changes with the C side's
[output format](#output-format): `native_traces=` reads whichever of the two
it wrote. The C side's own file (`trace_rank00000.h5` or `.spt`) is an
intermediate, left beside the result.

Because both APIs read the same clock, the C regions nest inside the Python
region that called them and `call_stack()` sees a single tree:

```
  python:setup                   11.970 ms   [python]
  python:timestep                 0.331 ms   [python]
    python:call_solver              0.320 ms   [python]
      c:stencil                       0.023 ms   [c]
      c:residual                      0.040 ms   [c]
```

Two rules:

- **Call the C `sp_finalize()` first.** Its output file has to exist by the
  time `finalize()` reads it.
- **Give the two sides distinct region names.** A name recorded by both raises,
  rather than silently double-counting a wrapper and the region inside it. A
  `python:` / `c:` prefix is the simplest convention.

### One ctypes trap

`ctypes` assumes a function returns `int` unless told otherwise, so a `double`
return comes back as garbage without `restype`. The regions are still recorded
correctly, which makes it easy to miss. Declare `argtypes` and `restype` for
everything you call.

## One timeline with Python

The API reads the same OS clock CPython's `time.perf_counter_ns()` uses —
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC` on Linux, `CLOCK_UPTIME_RAW` on macOS — resolved by probing
at run time.

The macOS case is worth knowing about if you ever vendor this file: defining
`_POSIX_C_SOURCE` there *hides* `CLOCK_UPTIME_RAW`, and the fallback
`CLOCK_MONOTONIC` is both microsecond-granular and on a different epoch. The
implementation therefore defines `_DARWIN_C_SOURCE` on Apple platforms and
`_POSIX_C_SOURCE` elsewhere — for opposite reasons on each.

## The trace format

This is the `.spt` fallback format; a build with HDF5 writes the schema
described in {doc}`hdf5_and_python_api` instead. Compatible with the Fortran
API's; see {doc}`fortran` for the shared layout.
16 bytes per recorded call, the same as the Python side. The C API writes
format version 2, adding an optional source file and line per region (empty
when a region was registered with `sp_region()` rather than
`sp_region_at()`); the Fortran API still writes version 1, with no source
field at all. Both versions are readable from the same trace directory, so a
mixed C/Fortran run still merges into one profile.

## Limitations

- **Not thread safe.** A region must be entered and left by the same thread.
  OpenMP threads inside a region are fine — wrap the whole parallel construct
  in one `sp_begin`/`sp_end` from the master thread.
- **Counter storage is owned by LIKWID.** Native C++ scopes write the ordinary
  timing output and LIKWID writes its marker output; neither native format
  carries counters.
- **The HDF5 output is timing-only**, like the trace: no GPU durations, no
  line profile, no per-call parent ids. Post-processing reconstructs the call
  graph and exclusive times from the recorded intervals, exactly as it does
  for an imported trace.
- **Recursion depth** per region is capped at `SP_MAX_DEPTH` (64); deeper
  nesting is reported on stderr and left untimed rather than corrupting the
  buffer.
- **A region still open at `sp_finalize()`** is reported on stderr and dropped,
  rather than written with a missing end time.
